title: The Economics of Ecosystems and Biodiversity
article: The Economics of Ecosystems and Biodiversity

definition.text: TEEB was an international study, led by Pavan Sukhdev from 2007 to 2011, that set out to show the global economic benefits of biodiversity and the rising cost of losing it.

facts.text: Germany and the European Commission launched TEEB in 2007, answering a proposal by G8+5 environment ministers meeting in Potsdam for a global study of the economics of biodiversity loss.
Its 2008 interim report focused largely on forests and put the loss of natural capital from deforestation and degradation at US$2–4.5 trillion per year.
It estimated that investing US$45 billion a year in protected areas alone could secure ecosystem services worth some US$5 trillion a year.
Phase II was presented in October 2010 at the 10th Conference of the Parties of the Convention on Biological Diversity in Nagoya, Japan.
A central aim was an economic yardstick better than GDP, and national accounts broad enough to measure the welfare benefits ecosystems provide.
TEEB reported that ecosystem service values run from about $100 per hectare per year for open ocean to over $1,000,000 per hectare per year for the richest coral reefs.
Critics argue that basing nature's value on human preferences cannot tell us what is ecologically essential to keep life-support systems working.

contested_note: Critics dispute whether valuing ecosystems by human preferences, as TEEB does, can guide what nature must be protected.

title: Stockholm Conference of 1972
article: United Nations Conference on the Human Environment

definition.text: The United Nations Conference on the Human Environment, held in Stockholm from 5 to 16 June 1972, was the first global conference on environmental issues.

facts.text: Sweden proposed the idea to the UN Economic and Social Council in 1968, and preparations took four years, involved 114 governments and cost over $30,000,000.
The conference created the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP), the first UN agency headquartered in a developing country, in Nairobi.
It agreed a Declaration of 26 principles on environment and development, an Action Plan of 109 recommendations, and a Resolution.
Divisions between rich and poor countries surfaced; developing countries made up 70 of the 122 countries attending, while the Soviet bloc boycotted it.
Indira Gandhi's speech linked ecological management with relieving poverty, which became one of the conference's central themes.
It spurred countries to monitor their environments and set up environment ministries and agencies.
The 1992 Rio Earth Summit, the 2002 Johannesburg summit and Rio+20 in 2012 all took the Stockholm declaration as their starting point.

title: Earth Summit

definition.text: The Earth Summit was the United Nations Conference on Environment and Development, held in Rio de Janeiro from 3 to 14 June 1992.

facts.text: It was attended by 108 heads of state and government and helped establish and spread the idea of sustainable development.
A key achievement was the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change, signed by 154 states, which later led to the Kyoto Protocol and the Paris Agreement.
The Convention on Biological Diversity was opened for signature at the summit.
It produced the Rio Declaration and Agenda 21, which 178 governments voted to adopt, and set up the Commission on Sustainable Development to oversee them.
It helped spread key treaty principles: the precautionary principle, common but differentiated responsibilities, and the polluter pays principle.
Critics note that many Rio agreements, on fighting poverty and cleaning up the environment, were never realized, and some leaders called it green imperialism by the global North.

related: United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change

definition.text: Our Common Future, or the Brundtland Report, is the 1987 report of the UN's World Commission on Environment and Development that set out the best-known definition of sustainable development.

facts.text: It defined sustainable development as development that meets present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.
It treated environment and development as one single issue and stressed the interlocking economic, environmental and social sides of human development.
It held that poverty worsens environmental pressure, and recognized that environmental limits to economic growth exist.
The report came out of a 900-day worldwide exercise of public hearings and expert testimony, chaired by former Norwegian Prime Minister Gro Harlem Brundtland.
It laid the groundwork for the 1992 Earth Summit, Agenda 21 and the Rio Declaration.
In 1988 Helge Ole Bergesen wrote that Third World elites saw the report as green imperialism.
